content: Chemotherapeutic agents like topotecan are utilized as salvage treatments for epithelial ovarian carcinoma (EOC). However, the therapeutic effects of topotecan have not been systematically reviewed before. This study aimed to assess the effectiveness and safety of topotecan in treating ovarian cancer. A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, the European Organization for the Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) database, and the Chinese Biomedical Database (CBM), covering studies from January 1990 to September 2015. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared topotecan, either alone or in combination, to interventions without topotecan were included. Data extraction and analysis were performed independently by two reviewers. The review included six multicenter pre-market RCTs involving 5,640 participants. Three studies were deemed to have a low risk of bias, while the remaining three had unclear or moderate risk due to insufficient reporting. Survival outcomes were inconsistently reported across studies, and differences in participant characteristics and comparisons prevented data pooling. The median overall survival (OS) for patients treated with topotecan ranged from 39.6 weeks to 63 weeks across the studies. One study focused on women with primary advanced-stage ovarian cancer, while the others involved women with relapsed ovarian cancer. No significant difference in OS was observed when comparing topotecan to paclitaxel (P = 0.44) or topotecan plus thalidomide (P = 0.67). Similarly, no significant OS difference was found when comparing topotecan to pegylated liposomal doxorubicin (PLD) (P = 0.341). However, in the platinum-sensitive subgroup of the PLD study, topotecan was associated with a shorter median survival time compared to PLD (70 weeks versus 108 weeks). Topotecan demonstrated significantly longer OS compared to treosulfan (P = 0.0023). Median progression-free survival (PFS) with topotecan ranged from 16 to 23 weeks. No statistically significant difference in PFS was observed when comparing topotecan to PLD (P = 0.095). In one of two studies comparing topotecan to paclitaxel, topotecan delayed disease progression more effectively (median 14 weeks versus 23.1 weeks; Risk Ratio [RR] 0.587, P = 0.0021). Similarly, topotecan showed better PFS compared to treosulfan (median 12.7 weeks versus 23.1 weeks, P = 0.0020). However, PFS was significantly shorter for topotecan alone compared to topotecan combined with thalidomide (four months versus six months, P = 0.02). One study comparing topotecan to no further treatment found no significant differences in OS (P = 0.30) or PFS (Hazard Ratio [HR] 1.07, P = 0.31). Topotecan was associated with more severe hematological toxicity compared to paclitaxel (RR 1.03 to 14.46), PLD (RR 1.73 to 27.12), and treosulfan (50% versus 12%). The quality of evidence ranged from low to moderate. In conclusion, for women with platinum-resistant ovarian cancer, topotecan may be as effective as paclitaxel and PLD in terms of OS and may delay disease progression more effectively than paclitaxel. However, additional evidence is required. The combination of topotecan and thalidomide appears to delay progression more effectively than topotecan alone, but it does not improve OS. Topotecan shows improved survival compared to treosulfan. For women with platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer, topotecan appears less effective than PLD, and its use after carboplatin and paclitaxel does not provide additional survival benefits. Severe hematological toxicity is a significant concern with topotecan and must be considered when evaluating treatment options. Large, high-quality post-market RCTs are necessary to confirm the efficacy and safety of topotecan.
